claim: The data set included the names of more than 9000 editors, 43,000 reviewers, and 126,000 authors for about 41,000 articles published in 142 journals in Science, Health, Engineering and the Humanities and Social Sciences.
source: This data set included the names of more than 9000 editors, 43,000 reviewers, and 126,000 authors for about 41,000 articles published in 142 journals in Science, Health, Engineering and the Humanities and Social Sciences (see Materials and methods).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific numbers extracted from the Frontiers journals dataset.

claim: The data set is one of the largest available to date, containing at least an order of magnitude more information than most data sets used in previous studies of peer review.
source: This data set is one of the largest available to date, and contains at least an order of magnitude more information than most data sets used in previous studies of peer review (see Supplementary file 2 for comparison).
evidence: The manuscript compares the dataset size to previous studies and references a supplementary file for detailed comparison.

claim: Women are underrepresented in the peer-review process.
source: Here, using public information about the identities of 9000 editors and 43000 reviewers from the Frontiers series of journals, we show that women are underrepresented in the peer-review process
evidence: The abstract states this as a main finding based on analysis of the dataset.

claim: Editors of both genders operate with substantial same-gender preference (homophily).
source: that editors of both genders operate with substantial same-gender preference (homophily)
evidence: The abstract presents this as a key finding from the analysis.

claim: The mechanisms of homophily are gender-dependent.
source: and that the mechanisms of this homophily are gender-dependent.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding from the analysis.

claim: Homophily will persist even if numerical parity between genders is reached.
source: We also show that homophily will persist even if numerical parity between genders is reached
evidence: The abstract presents this as a conclusion from the analysis.

claim: The peer-reviewing interactions in the Frontiers journal series gave rise to a mature, topologically stable and integrated community.
source: Thus, peer-reviewing interactions in the Frontiers journal series gave rise to a mature, topologically stable and integrated community, even though its contributors constitute only a small subset of researchers worldwide.
evidence: The manuscript presents network analysis metrics showing stability over time.

claim: The fractions of authoring, reviewing and editing contributions by women amounted to 37%, 28% and 26%, respectively, in the complete accumulated data until 2015.
source: Figure 1b reveals that the fractions of authoring, reviewing and editing contributions by women — amounting to 37%, 28% and 26%, respectively, in the complete accumulated data until 2015
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages from the data analysis.

claim: The fractions of authoring, reviewing and editing contributions by women are always significantly smaller than the corresponding fractions for men.
source: Figure 1b reveals that the fractions of authoring, reviewing and editing contributions by women — amounting to 37%, 28% and 26%, respectively, in the complete accumulated data until 2015 — are always significantly smaller than the corresponding fractions for men.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing gender disparities across all roles.

claim: The unbalance between male and female contributions worsens when gradually ascending through the peer-review hierarchy.
source: The unbalance between male and female contributions thus worsens when gradually ascending through the peer-review hierarchy.
evidence: The manuscript shows decreasing percentages of women from authors (37%) to reviewers (28%) to editors (26%).

claim: Linear extrapolation based on the fractions observed from 2012 to 2015 would predict that exact parity could be achieved as late as 2027 for authoring, 2034 for reviewing and 2042 for editing.
source: Linear extrapolation based on the fractions observed from 2012 to 2015 would predict that exact parity could be achieved as late as 2027 for authoring, 2034 for reviewing and 2042 for editing.
evidence: The manuscript provides projections based on trend analysis of the data.

claim: Author and reviewing contributions by women lay significantly below the confidence intervals obtained through permutation testing since 2009 and 2011, respectively.
source: Author and reviewing contributions by women lay significantly below the confidence intervals obtained through this permutation testing procedure since 2009 and 2011, respectively.
evidence: The manuscript describes statistical testing results comparing actual data to gender-blind null hypothesis.

claim: The mere overall smaller number of female actors cannot explain the observed unbalanced fractions of female contributions to the peer-review chain.
source: Thus, the mere overall smaller number of female actors cannot explain the observed unbalanced fractions of female contributions to the peer-review chain.
evidence: The manuscript concludes this from permutation testing that controls for numerical representation.

claim: Women had a significantly smaller than chance probability to review (and author) more than one article.
source: women had a significantly smaller than chance probability to review (and author) more than one article, while their probability to act as single-time reviewer or author exceeded the expected chance level
evidence: The manuscript presents distribution analysis comparing observed data to chance expectations.

claim: Women's probability to act as single-time reviewer or author exceeded the expected chance level.
source: women had a significantly smaller than chance probability to review (and author) more than one article, while their probability to act as single-time reviewer or author exceeded the expected chance level
evidence: The manuscript presents distribution analysis comparing observed data to chance expectations.

claim: 73% of reviewers appointed by men were also men.
source: Specifically, 73% of reviewers appointed by men were also men
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages from network analysis.

claim: 33% of reviewers appointed by women were women.
source: 33% of reviewers appointed by women were women
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages from network analysis.

claim: Both the percentages of same-gender appointments by male and female editors laid above the expectations drawn from the assumption that genders were randomly distributed in the given editor-to-reviewer network topology.
source: but, importantly, both these numbers laid above the expectations drawn from the assumption that genders were randomly distributed in the given editor-to-reviewer network topology.
evidence: The manuscript compares observed percentages to statistical expectations from null hypothesis.

claim: Male (female) reviewers assessed articles authored by male (female) authors significantly more often than expected.
source: Similarly, in the reviewer-to-author network (Figure 3b), male (female) reviewers assessed articles authored by male (female) authors significantly more often than expected.
evidence: The manuscript presents analysis of the reviewer-to-author network showing homophily.

claim: Homophily is widespread across scientific fields, including those with relatively mild underrepresentation of women.
source: We first checked for the influence of local subnetwork structure on apparent gender bias by looking at different scientific fields, including those with relatively mild underrepresentation of women, and found homophily widespread across disciplines (Figure 3c).
evidence: The manuscript analyzes different disciplinary groupings and finds consistent patterns.

claim: Male (female) editors generally appointed female reviewers at a lower (higher) rate than expected even at the local neighborhood level.
source: Even at this local neighborhood level, we continued to find that male (female) editors generally appointed female reviewers at a lower (higher) rate than expected.
evidence: The manuscript presents analysis controlling for local network structure.

claim: For male editors, most histogram bins for Φhom < 0.6 displayed node counts significantly larger than gender-shuffled estimations.
source: For male editors, most histogram bins for Φhom < 0.6 displayed node counts significantly larger than gender-shuffled estimations.
evidence: The manuscript presents analysis of inbreeding homophily index distributions.

claim: It was enough to remove the few most homophilic female editors with the lowest values of Φhom from the network to bring the probability for a female editor to appoint a female reviewer back to chance-level.
source: On the one hand, we found that it was enough to remove the few most homophilic female editors with the lowest values of Φhom from the network, to bring the probability for a female editor to appoint a female reviewer back to chance-level.
evidence: The manuscript presents results from pruning analysis of the network.

claim: The probability for a male editor to appoint a female reviewer remained significantly below chance expectations for all the considered thresholds for inclusion, 0 ≤ Φthr ≤ 0.5.
source: In particular, it remained significantly below chance expectations for all the considered thresholds for inclusion, 0 ≤ Φthr ≤ 0.5.
evidence: The manuscript presents results from pruning analysis showing persistent bias.

claim: The overall smaller-than-chance probability of appointing female reviewers for male editors is due to inbreeding homophilic tendencies that are widespread among male editors.
source: This means that the overall smaller-than-chance probability of appointing female reviewers for male editors is due to inbreeding homophilic tendencies that are widespread among male editors, although at varying degrees of strength.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the pruning analysis results.

claim: The overall larger-than-chance probability to appoint female reviewers for female editors is driven by the action of just a small number of strongly homophilic female editors.
source: In contrast, the overall larger-than-chance probability to appoint female reviewers for female editors is driven by the action of just a small number of strongly homophilic female editors, with most other female editors showing only "passive" baseline homophily.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the pruning analysis results.

claim: The number of female doctoral recipients at US institutions increased by, on average, 0.1% - 0.6% per year between 2005 and 2015, depending on broad field of study.
source: The number of female doctoral recipients at US institutions increased by, on average, 0.1% - 0.6% per year between 2005 and 2015, depending on broad field of study (National Science Foundation, 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites external data from the National Science Foundation.

claim: The number of fraction of women in medical schools increased by, on average, 0.6% to 0.8% per year between 1996 and 2007.
source: Ley and Hamilton (2008) reported that the number of fraction of women in medical schools increased by, on average, 0.6% to 0.8% per year (depending on the scientists' rank) between 1996 and 2007.
evidence: The manuscript cites findings from Ley and Hamilton (2008).

claim: Percentages of women professors has increased at a rate of 0.5%-1% per year in the European Union.
source: Percentages of women professors has increased at a rate of 0.5%-1% per year in the European Union (ETAN Expert Working Group on Women and Science,ETAN Expert Working Group on Women and Science, 2000).
evidence: The manuscript cites data from the ETAN Expert Working Group report.

claim: The fraction of publishing female scientists in Germany increased by, on average 0.7% from 2010 to 2014, it is now 30.9%.
source: The fraction of publishing female scientists in Germany increased by, on average 0.7% from 2010 to 2014, it is now 30.9% (Pan and Kalinaki, 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites data from Pan and Kalinaki (2015).

claim: The number of female first authors of astronomy articles increased by about 0.4% per year between 1960 and 2015.
source: Caplar et al. (2016) noted that the number of female first authors of astronomy articles increased by about 0.4% per year between 1960 and 2015.
evidence: The manuscript cites findings from Caplar et al. (2016).

claim: In the Frontiers series of journals, the number of contributions by female authors, reviewers and editors increased by, on average, 1.1% / year, 1.2% / year and 0.9% / year between 2012 and 2015, respectively.
source: In the Frontiers series of journals, we found that the number of contributions by female authors, reviewers and editors increased by, on average, 1.1% / year, 1.2% / year and 0.9% / year between 2012 and 2015, respectively, similar to the numbers above.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific rates of change from their data analysis.

claim: Women are generally less productive than men measured by their number of publications.
source: Previous studies reported that, measured by their number of publications, women are generally less productive than men (Cole and Zuckerman, 1984; Zuckerman, 1991; Long and Fox, 1995; Xie and Shauman, 1998; Pan and Kalinaki, 2015; Caplar et al., 2016)
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple previous studies reporting this finding.

claim: The fraction of female scientists decreases with rank or age.
source: Moreover, the fraction of female scientists decreases with rank or age (ETAN Expert Working Group on Women and Science, 2000; Ley and Hamilton, 2008; Goulden et al., 2011)
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies reporting this pattern.

claim: Women with children are not less productive than those without.
source: Also, it has been reported that women with children are not less productive than those without (Hamovitch and Morgenstern, 1977; Cole, 1979; Cole and Zuckerman, 1987)
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies reporting this finding.

claim: Young children might decrease productivity.
source: although young children might decrease productivity (Kyvik, 1990; Kyvik and Teigen, 1996).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies reporting this finding.

claim: The implicit association of "male" and "science" is strongest in the group of 40-65 year olds.
source: as the implicit association of "male" and "science" is strongest in the group of 40-65 year olds (Nosek et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites findings from Nosek et al. (2007).

claim: Female editors have been reported to be more productive than male editors.
source: On the other hand, a compensating factor seems to be that female editors, in contrast to authors, have been reported to be more productive than male editors (Gilbert et al., 1994).
evidence: The manuscript cites findings from Gilbert et al. (1994).

claim: Men and women who are invited to review a manuscript have very similar propensities to accept the invitation.
source: Interestingly, men and women who are invited to review a manuscript have very similar propensities to accept the invitation (Fox et al., 2016; Lerback and Hanson, 2017)
evidence: The manuscript cites findings from Fox et al. (2016) and Lerback and Hanson (2017).

claim: Women have been reported to be less likely to be hired.
source: Women have been reported to be less likely to be hired (Moss-Racusin et al., 2012)
evidence: The manuscript cites findings from Moss-Racusin et al. (2012).

claim: Women have been reported to be less likely to receive a grant.
source: to receive a grant (Wennerås and Wold, 1997)
evidence: The manuscript cites findings from Wennerås and Wold (1997).

claim: Women have been reported to receive lower salaries.
source: and to receive higher salaries (Shen, 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites findings from Shen (2013).

claim: Most people implicitly associate science with men, and liberal arts with women more than the other way round.
source: Still today, most people implicitly associate science with men, and liberal arts with women more than the other way round (Nosek et al., 2007)
evidence: The manuscript cites findings from Nosek et al. (2007).

claim: The tendency to associate science with men is apparent from a very young age.
source: and this tendency, for both men and women, is apparent from a very young age (del Río and Strasser, 2013; Bian et al., 2017)
evidence: The manuscript cites findings from del Río and Strasser (2013) and Bian et al. (2017).

claim: Men are more reluctant than women to believe that gender bias exists.
source: Beyond that, men are more reluctant than women to believe that such a bias exists (Handley et al., 2015a)
evidence: The manuscript cites findings from Handley et al. (2015a).

claim: 42% of authors in scientific articles analyzed by Larivière et al. (2013) were women.
source: They reported that 42% of authors in their analyzed scientific articles were women, whereas we found that number to be 39% in the Frontiers journals.
evidence: The manuscript compares their findings to those of Larivière et al. (2013).

claim: 39% of authors in the Frontiers journals were women.
source: They reported that 42% of authors in their analyzed scientific articles were women, whereas we found that number to be 39% in the Frontiers journals.
evidence: The manuscript provides this percentage from their data analysis.

claim: Only 9% of editors in 435 mathematical journals were women.
source: Larger sample sizes, but limited to editors, were considered in an analysis of the composition of editorial boards of 435 mathematical journals (Topaz and Sen, 2016). Only 9% of editors were women.
evidence: The manuscript cites findings from Topaz and Sen (2016).

claim: The fraction of women editors across the Frontiers journals ranges between 6% (Frontiers in Robotics and AI) and 37% (Frontiers in Aging Neuroscience), with an average of 28%.
source: These numbers lie at the lower and upper end of the female editor fractions across the Frontiers journals, ranging between 6% (Frontiers in Robotics and AI) and 37% (Frontiers in Aging Neuroscience), with an average of 28%.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages from their data analysis.

claim: The fraction of female reviewers or female reviewer appointments across the Frontiers journals ranges between 11% and 48% with an average of 30%.
source: Concerning female reviewers or female reviewer appointments, fractions reported in the literature range between 16% and 48% (cf. Supplementary file 2), to be compared with the range between 11% and 48% for the Frontiers journals with an average of 30%.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages from their data analysis.

claim: Female author fractions in Frontiers journals range from 17% (Neurorobotics) to 48% (Public Health).
source: These numbers are once again comparable to female author fractions in Frontiers journals, ranging from 17% (Neurorobotics) to 48% (Public Health).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages from their data analysis.

claim: The probability that a female editor appoints a female reviewer was reported to be 31%-33%, whereas male editors appointed female reviewers in 22%-27% of cases.
source: The probability that a female editor appoints a female reviewer was reported to be 31%-33%, whereas male editors appointed female reviewers in 22%-27% of cases (Gilbert et al., 1994; Buckley et al., 2014; Fox et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites findings from previous studies.

claim: For the whole spectrum of Frontiers journals, the probability that a female editor appoints a female reviewer is 33% and male editors appoint female reviewers in 27% of cases.
source: Here, for the whole spectrum of Frontiers journals we found these numbers to be similar: 33% and 27%, respectively.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages from their data analysis.

claim: Gender homophily has been found in groups of playing children.
source: Since the classic studies of Park and Burgess (1921) and Lazarsfeld and Merton (1954), gender homophily has been found in groups of playing children (Bott, 1928; Shrum et al., 1988)
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on homophily in social contexts.

claim: Gender homophily has been found in adult friends.
source: and adult friends (Verbrugge, 1977)
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on homophily in social contexts.

claim: Gender homophily is present in work environments.
source: and is also present in work environments (Brass, 1985; Bielby and Baron, 1986; Ibarra, 1992)
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on homophily in social contexts.

claim: Gender homophily is present in voluntary organizations.
source: and voluntary organizations (Popielarz, 1999).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on homophily in social contexts.

claim: Professional social networks of men are more homophilic than women's, especially in work environments in which men are dominant.
source: Professional social networks of men are more homophilic than women's, especially in work environments in which men are dominant (Brass, 1985; Ibarra, 1992).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on gender differences in homophily.

claim: Both men and women tend to form connection routes passing through a male node when reaching toward distant domains.
source: Another source of asymmetry may be that both men and women tend to form connection routes passing through a male node when reaching toward distant domains (Aldrich, 1989).
evidence: The manuscript cites findings from Aldrich (1989).

claim: A stronger involvement of women would increase the quality of scientific output.
source: Altogether, inbreeding homophily negatively affects science as a whole because a stronger involvement of women would increase the quality of scientific output (Merton, 1973; Woolley et al., 2010; Nature, 2013; Campbell et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies supporting this claim.

claim: The data set included information about authors in 41,092 articles, about reviewers in 39,788 articles, and about editors in 40,405 articles.
source: Our parsing routine was able to find information about authors in 41'092 of these articles, about reviewers in 39'788 articles (note that some articles, like editorial articles, might not have been reviewed), and about editors in 40'405 articles.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific numbers from their data collection process.

claim: 71% of contributors were associated with an official profile identification number in the Frontiers database.
source: When a contributor was found to be associated to an official profile identification number in the Frontiers database, then we relied on it, directly translating it into a UID (this happened for 71% of contributors).
evidence: The manuscript provides this percentage from their data processing.

claim: At least one first name was fully specified for 99.6% of the UIDs.
source: note that after the steps described in the previous section, at least one first name was fully specified for 99.6% of the UIDs, while for the remaining 0.4% of UIDs all given names consisted of only initials so that no gender could be attributed
evidence: The manuscript provides this percentage from their data processing.

claim: The gender automatically assigned by the algorithm was correct in 96% of cases based on validation of 924 randomly selected people.
source: We were able to find such information for 924 out of the 1053 people (88%). The gender automatically assigned by our algorithm to those identified was correct in 96 % of cases.
evidence: The manuscript provides validation results for their gender assignment method.

claim: The name-gender algorithm used in Larivière et al. (2013) misclassified male and female names in 8% of cases.
source: For comparison, we note that the name-gender algorithm used in Larivière et al. (2013) misclassified male and female names in 8% of cases.
evidence: The manuscript cites the error rate from Larivière et al. (2013) for comparison.

claim: The name list comprised 66605 female and 43482 male names.
source: Our list thus comprised 66605 female and 43482 male names.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific numbers from their name list compilation.

claim: Gender was assigned to 131885, that is 87% of UIDs.
source: In total, we were thereby able to assign gender to 131885, that is 87 % of UIDs.
evidence: The manuscript provides this percentage from their data processing.

claim: The weak giant component of the latest reviewer-to-author network reaches 95% of its global size.
source: The latest reviewer-to-author (editor-to-reviewer) network sampled at the cutoff date has a giant component reaching 95% (93%) of its global size.
evidence: The manuscript provides network analysis metrics shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The weak giant component of the latest editor-to-reviewer network reaches 93% of its global size.
source: The latest reviewer-to-author (editor-to-reviewer) network sampled at the cutoff date has a giant component reaching 95% (93%) of its global size.
evidence: The manuscript provides network analysis metrics shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: 39% of all available authors were women.
source: overall there are numerically less female than male authors, reviewers and editors (39%, 30% and 28% out of all available authors, reviewers and editors, respectively, were women, closely mirroring the observed fractions of assignments).
evidence: The manuscript provides this percentage from their data analysis.

claim: 30% of all available reviewers were women.
source: overall there are numerically less female than male authors, reviewers and editors (39%, 30% and 28% out of all available authors, reviewers and editors, respectively, were women, closely mirroring the observed fractions of assignments).
evidence: The manuscript provides this percentage from their data analysis.

claim: 28% of all available editors were women.
source: overall there are numerically less female than male authors, reviewers and editors (39%, 30% and 28% out of all available authors, reviewers and editors, respectively, were women, closely mirroring the observed fractions of assignments).
evidence: The manuscript provides this percentage from their data analysis.

claim: The number of contributions by female authors varies between about 15% (Frontiers in Neurorobotics) and 50% (Public Health).
source: Overall, the number of contributions by female authors varies between about 15% (Frontiers in Neurorobotics) and 50% (Public Health)
evidence: The manuscript provides this range from their data analysis.

claim: The number of contributions by female reviewers varies between about 15% (Surgery) and 50% (Public Health).
source: by female reviewers between about 15% (Surgery) and 50% (Public Health)
evidence: The manuscript provides this range from their data analysis.

claim: The number of contributions by female editors varies from ca. 5% (Robotics AI) to 35% (Aging Neuroscience).
source: and by female editors from ca. 5% (Robotics AI) to 35% (Aging Neuroscience).
evidence: The manuscript provides this range from their data analysis.

claim: Peer review is the cornerstone of scholarly publishing.
source: Peer review is the cornerstone of scholarly publishing and it is essential that peer reviewers are appointed on the basis of their expertise alone.
evidence: The manuscript states this as an established principle.

claim: It is essential that peer reviewers are appointed on the basis of their expertise alone.
source: Peer review is the cornerstone of scholarly publishing and it is essential that peer reviewers are appointed on the basis of their expertise alone.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a normative principle.

claim: The identity of peer reviewers generally remains confidential.
source: However, it is difficult to check for any bias in the peer-review process because the identity of peer reviewers generally remains confidential.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a general practice in scholarly publishing.

claim: Frontiers journals generally disclose the identities of peer reviewers and associate editors alongside each published article.
source: Frontiers journals (www.frontiersin.org) differ from most journals in that they generally disclose the identities of peer reviewers and associate editors alongside each published article in an attempt to increase the transparency and quality of the publication process (Poynder, 2016).
evidence: The manuscript describes the unique practice of Frontiers journals.

claim: Inbreeding homophily is an active preference to connect with same-gender network nodes, on top of baseline homophily.
source: Both independent analyses – by topic or localized – validate the existence of a so-called "inbreeding" homophily, i.e. an active preference to connect with same-gender network nodes, on top of "baseline" homophily (McPherson et al., 2001).
evidence: The manuscript defines inbreeding homophily and cites McPherson et al. (2001).

claim: Baseline homophily is subtle but unavoidable bias caused by disproportions in the number of reachable male and female nodes due to heterogeneous network structure.
source: While these findings seem to point at homophily created by choices, they might also stem from "baseline" homophily (McPherson et al., 2001), i.e. subtle but unavoidable bias caused by disproportions in the number of reachable male and female nodes due to heterogeneous network structure.
evidence: The manuscript defines baseline homophily and cites McPherson et al. (2001).

claim: The average shortest path length for the editor-to-reviewer network is 12 steps.
source: which is a short distance relative to the average shortest path length of 12 steps for the editor-to-reviewer network, cf Figure 1—figure supplement 1e
evidence: The manuscript provides this network metric from their analysis.

claim: Simply increasing the number of invitations to female reviewers would have a direct and proportional effect on the number of female reviews.
source: Interestingly, men and women who are invited to review a manuscript have very similar propensities to accept the invitation (Fox et al., 2016; Lerback and Hanson, 2017), suggesting: (1) that simply increasing the number of invitations to female reviewers would have a direct and proportional effect
evidence: The manuscript infers this implication from the cited finding about similar acceptance rates.

claim: The low number of female reviews in the data is caused in part by a lower number of invitations.
source: and, (2) that the low number of female reviews in our data is caused in part by a lower number of invitations.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the finding that acceptance rates are similar between genders.

claim: The underrepresentation and discrimination of women in the scientific community is a problem that will not solve by itself.
source: The underrepresentation and discrimination of women in the scientific community is a problem that will not solve by itself, given the pervasive, generally unconscious nature of gender bias.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a conclusion based on the evidence presented.

claim: Gender bias is pervasive and generally unconscious.
source: The underrepresentation and discrimination of women in the scientific community is a problem that will not solve by itself, given the pervasive, generally unconscious nature of gender bias.
evidence: The manuscript characterizes gender bias based on the literature and findings.

claim: Inbreeding homophily is likely not restricted to the peer review of manuscripts.
source: The phenomenon of inbreeding homophily is also likely not restricted to the peer review of manuscripts, so it needs to be taken into account for grant evaluation, hiring, or when designing mentoring programs.
evidence: The manuscript speculates about broader implications of their findings.

claim: Inbreeding homophily needs to be taken into account for grant evaluation, hiring, or when designing mentoring programs.
source: The phenomenon of inbreeding homophily is also likely not restricted to the peer review of manuscripts, so it needs to be taken into account for grant evaluation, hiring, or when designing mentoring programs.
evidence: The manuscript recommends this based on their findings about homophily in peer review.

claim: Raising awareness seems to be the most promising route to combat inbreeding homophily.
source: As inbreeding homophily is an expression of a state of mind it is likely little amenable to change by externally enforced measures. Raising awareness, in comparison, seems to be the most promising route.
evidence: The manuscript argues for this approach based on the nature of homophily.

claim: Removing the authors' names is often not sufficiently blinding in peer review.
source: First of all, removing the authors' names is often not sufficiently blinding. References to the authors' previous publications or to the approving ethics committee all but spell out the authors.
evidence: The manuscript discusses limitations of blind review based on common knowledge.

claim: An editorial management software is the ideal platform to routinely direct the editor's attention to the issue of homophily.
source: an editorial management software is also the ideal platform to routinely direct the editor's attention to the issue of homophily.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this as a potential solution.
